title: Oxygen delivery devices, titration and weaning
blurb: Match the device and flow to the patient, titrate safely against the target and wean oxygen off without rebound hypoxaemia.
question: Mrs Kaur, 58, recovering from pneumonia, has been at 97–98% on 2 L/min nasal cannulae for the last 6 hours and is clinically stable. Her target is 94–98%. What should the nurse do with her oxygen and her prescription?

teach.h: Device, flow and target work together
teach.body: Formally: the delivery device and flow rate are adjusted to keep the patient's saturation within the prescribed target range, and each change is recorded (BTS 2017). In plain English: the prescription gives you the destination (the range); the device and flow are how you drive there. Low-flow devices suit most patients, controlled devices suit people at risk of hypercapnia, and a reservoir mask is for very low saturations and critical illness.
teach.cite: BTS guideline for oxygen use in adults 2017, sections W and U

teach.caption: Chart abbreviations: N 2 L/min (nasal), SM (simple mask), RM 15 L/min (reservoir), V24, V28 (Venturi).
BTS: increasing the flow into a Venturi mask does not increase the oxygen concentration delivered; extra flow compensates for a high inspiratory flow.

teach.body: Increase oxygen if saturation is below the target range and decrease it if above (BTS W10). After any change, record the new saturation, device and flow on the observation chart after 5 minutes at the new setting (W11). A patient who needs more oxygen to stay in range needs prompt clinical review, and an at-risk patient needs repeat blood gases 30–60 minutes after a change.

steps.sub: stable and above target, or upper zone 4–8 h

steps.sub: to 2 L/min nasal (1 L/min if at risk)

steps.sub: in range on two consecutive observations

teach.note: Sudden cessation in a patient who is retaining CO2 can cause life-threatening rebound hypoxaemia, so step down rather than stopping abruptly.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Kaur on a medical ward
teach.body: Mrs Kaur has been at 97–98% (the upper zone of 94–98%) on 2 L/min for 6 hours and is stable. Nurse Tomasz stops her oxygen, checks her SpO2 on air after 5 minutes (95%) and again at 1 hour (95%, NEWS2 unchanged). Oxygen is safely discontinued. He leaves the 94–98% target on the prescription chart so that oxygen can be restarted promptly if she deteriorates, and documents each step.

teach.text: Discontinuing oxygen does NOT mean crossing out the oxygen prescription. The target range stays prescribed in case of future deterioration and to guide NEWS2 scoring. And turning up the flow on a Venturi mask does not give a higher percentage: change the valve if a higher concentration is needed.

items: Nasal cannulae 2–6 L/min or simple mask 5–10 L/min for most; reservoir mask 15 L/min if SpO2 below 85% or critically ill.
At risk of hypercapnia: 24% Venturi 2–3 L/min, 28% Venturi 4 L/min or cannulae 1–2 L/min.
Record saturation, device and flow 5 minutes after every change; sign the drug chart each round.
Wean in steps, stop when in range on two observations, check at 5 minutes and 1 hour.
Leave the target range prescribed after stopping; never stop abruptly in someone retaining CO2.

summary: You can now choose a delivery device and flow to suit the patient and target, titrate and record changes correctly, and wean oxygen in safe steps. You also know to keep the target prescription in place and how to respond if saturation falls after stopping.

A.q: A patient at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure needs controlled oxygen before blood gases are available. Which setting is appropriate?
A.why: BTS 2017: for at-risk patients before gases, use a 24% Venturi mask at 2–3 L/min, a 28% Venturi mask at 4 L/min or nasal cannulae at 1–2 L/min, aiming for 88–92%.

whyNot.0: A reservoir mask delivers high concentrations and is used at 15 L/min for critical illness.
whyNot.1: A simple face mask gives an uncontrolled concentration and is not the at-risk choice.
whyNot.3: Nasal cannulae for at-risk patients are set at 1–2 L/min, not 4 L/min.

A.q: A nurse turns up the flow on a patient's 28% Venturi mask from 4 to 6 L/min. What effect does this have on the oxygen concentration delivered?
A.why: BTS 2017: increasing the oxygen flow rate into a Venturi mask does not increase the concentration delivered. Higher flow can help a patient breathing fast (RR above 30) by matching their inspiratory flow.

whyNot.0: The percentage is set by the Venturi valve, not the flow rate.
whyNot.3: Increasing flow does not dilute the oxygen below the valve setting.

A.q: After stopping oxygen in a stable patient, when should the nurse first check SpO2 on air?
A.why: BTS U5: monitor saturation on air for 5 minutes after stopping oxygen; if it remains in range, recheck at 1 hour.

whyNot.1: The first check is earlier, at 5 minutes; the next is at 1 hour.
whyNot.2: Waiting for routine observations could miss early desaturation.

B.q: A patient with a target of 94–98% has been stable at 98% on 4 L/min nasal cannulae for 6 hours. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue 4 L/min until the ward round
Reduce the oxygen flow and recheck SpO2
Stop oxygen and remove the prescription
B.why: BTS U1: reduce oxygen in a clinically stable patient whose saturation has been in the upper zone of the range for some time (usually 4–8 hours), then record the new saturation after 5 minutes (W11).

whyNot.0: Waiting is unnecessary; oxygen should be reduced when the patient is stable in the upper zone.
whyNot.2: A Venturi mask is for patients at risk of hypercapnia, not routine weaning.
whyNot.3: Oxygen is stepped down first, and the target prescription stays in place after stopping.

B.q: A man with a COPD exacerbation and a raised PCO2 needs a salbutamol nebuliser. How should it be given?
options: By reservoir mask at 15 L/min instead
Driven by air with nasal oxygen
B.why: NG115 and BTS R2: in hypercapnic or acidotic patients, nebulisers should be driven by compressed air, with supplementary oxygen by nasal cannulae to maintain 88–92%.

whyNot.0: Oxygen-driven nebulisers risk worsening hypercapnia in this patient.
whyNot.1: Oxygen at 6 L/min is the driving gas for asthma, not hypercapnic COPD.
whyNot.2: A reservoir mask is not a nebuliser and would give high-concentration oxygen.

B.q: A patient's SpO2 falls to 91% (target 94–98%) 5 minutes after oxygen is stopped. What should the nurse do?
options: Restart the lowest level that kept target
Restart at 15 L/min via a reservoir mask
Leave off oxygen and recheck it at 1 hour
Restart at 4 L/min until the next morning
B.why: BTS U7: if saturation falls below target on stopping, restart the lowest concentration that maintained the target, monitor for 5 minutes, and try discontinuing again later.

whyNot.1: High-concentration oxygen is not needed for a small fall in a stable patient.
whyNot.2: Saturation below target needs oxygen restarted now.
whyNot.3: The patient should go back to the lowest effective level, not an arbitrary higher one.

C.q: Mr Ayodele, 70, with COPD, is on a 24% Venturi mask with SpO2 90%. His respiratory rate rises to 34/min and SpO2 drifts to 88%. What adjustment fits BTS guidance first?
options: Switch to a reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Raise the Venturi flow by up to 50%
Change to nasal cannulae at 6 L/min
Change to a simple face mask at 10 L/min
C.why: BTS 2017: increase Venturi mask flow by up to 50% if the respiratory rate is above 30, so the mask keeps up with his inspiratory flow; he remains within 88–92% and needs clinical review.

whyNot.0: A reservoir mask would give uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen to an at-risk patient.
whyNot.2: 6 L/min by cannulae is far above the 1–2 L/min used for at-risk patients.
whyNot.3: A simple face mask gives uncontrolled oxygen and is not the controlled choice.

C.q: Mrs Lewis's oxygen was stopped this morning. At 1 hour her SpO2 on air is 95% and NEWS2 is unchanged. A colleague asks whether to discontinue the oxygen prescription. What is the best reply?
options: Yes, as she no longer needs oxygen
Yes, once a doctor reviews the chart
No, keep oxygen running at 1 L/min overnight
No, the target range stays prescribed
C.why: BTS: oxygen is discontinued once the patient keeps target saturation on air, but the prescription for a target range is left in place in case of future deterioration and to guide NEWS2.

whyNot.0: Removing the target prescription delays treatment if she deteriorates.
whyNot.1: The prescription should remain, whoever reviews it.
whyNot.2: She is in range on air, so continuing oxygen is unnecessary.

C.q: A stable patient with COPD and a target of 88–92% is being weaned. Which step-down setting is appropriate before stopping oxygen?
C.why: BTS U3: patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure may be stepped down to 1 L/min (or occasionally 0.5 L/min) via nasal cannulae, or a 24% Venturi mask at 2 L/min, before cessation.

whyNot.0: 3 L/min is higher than the usual at-risk step-down level.
whyNot.1: A simple face mask is not a controlled step-down device.
whyNot.3: A 28% Venturi mask is not the lowest step before stopping.

reteach.title: Like coming down a staircase
reteach.question: Think of weaning oxygen as walking down a staircase rather than jumping off it. What does each step look like?

blocks.body: Each time you reduce oxygen you go down one step, then pause for 5 minutes and look at the saturation. If the patient stays in range, write it down and wait. When they are stable on the bottom step (2 L/min nasal, or 1 L/min if at risk of hypercapnia) and in range on two observations in a row, you step off: stop the oxygen, check at 5 minutes and at 1 hour. The handrail, the target range on the chart, stays in place.

blocks.text: Jumping off (stopping high-flow oxygen suddenly) in a patient who is retaining CO2 can cause life-threatening rebound hypoxaemia.

explain.body: Most hypoxaemic adults: nasal cannulae 2–6 L/min or a simple face mask 5–10 L/min. SpO2 below 85% or critical illness: reservoir mask 15 L/min. At risk of hypercapnia: Venturi 24% or 28%, or cannulae 1–2 L/min.

test.q: What flow range does BTS give for a simple face mask?
test.why: BTS 2017 recommends a simple face mask at 5–10 L/min.

whyNot.0: 1–2 L/min is a nasal cannulae flow for at-risk patients.
whyNot.1: 2–4 L/min is within the nasal cannulae range.
whyNot.3: 15 L/min is the reservoir mask flow.

explain.body: A Venturi valve fixes the oxygen percentage. More flow does not raise the percentage, but if the respiratory rate is above 30, BTS advises raising the flow by up to 50% so the mask keeps up with the patient's breathing.

test.q: A patient on a 24% Venturi mask needs a higher oxygen concentration after senior review. What achieves this?
options: Doubling the flow on the 24% valve
Adding nasal cannulae under the mask
test.why: The concentration from a Venturi mask is set by its valve, so a higher concentration needs a different valve (e.g. 28%).

whyNot.1: More flow does not raise the Venturi concentration.
whyNot.2: Adding cannulae makes the dose unpredictable.
whyNot.3: Mask fit does not change the valve setting.

explain.body: After any change, record the new saturation, the device and the flow rate on the observation chart after 5 minutes at the new setting. Registered nurses sign the drug chart on each drug round for patients on oxygen.

test.q: A nurse reduces a patient's oxygen from 4 to 2 L/min. When should the new saturation be recorded?
test.why: BTS W11: record the new saturation, delivery system and flow rate after 5 minutes of treatment at the new concentration.

whyNot.0: 1 minute is too early for the saturation to settle.
whyNot.3: 1 hour is the recheck after stopping oxygen, not after a change.

explain.body: Stop oxygen when the patient is clinically stable on low-concentration oxygen and saturation is in range on two consecutive observations. Check SpO2 on air at 5 minutes and at 1 hour. Leave the target range prescribed.

test.q: When does BTS advise that oxygen can be stopped in a stable patient on low-concentration oxygen?
options: When SpO2 is in range on one reading
When SpO2 is in range on two in a row
When SpO2 is above 98% on one reading
When the patient says they feel better
test.why: BTS U4: stop oxygen once the patient is clinically stable on low-concentration oxygen and saturation is within the desired range on two consecutive observations.

whyNot.0: One reading is not enough to show stability.
whyNot.2: A single high reading is not the stopping criterion.
whyNot.3: Feeling better is not an objective measure of oxygenation.
